manifesto.title: Intelligence is a craft, not a trick.
manifesto.lede: Deep learning is cheap to imitate and expensive to mean. My practice sits at the transfer point: the nervous boundary between a model that classifies and a system that actually helps.
paragraphs: I started with pixels. When I first watched a convolutional network learn to tell one face from the next, I stopped seeing vision as perception and started seeing it as a discipline — annotation, pre-processing, augmentation, patience. Everything I build now begins there.

The second lesson came from a hand. Building a real-time sign-language translator meant confronting the difference between a notebook accuracy of 92% and a classroom where the lighting is wrong, the hands are fast, and the frame rate fights you. Accuracy is necessary. Robustness is required.

I am drawn to work that sits just beyond the demo: deepfake detection that can be scrutinised, stroke risk models that clinicians could trust, assistants that remember context. I do not chase benchmarks for their own sake. I chase systems that survive contact with the real world.

This portfolio is arranged as a small magazine rather than a list — an index of work, a few convictions, and the record of a studio still learning. I am finishing a B.Tech in Computer Science (AI & ML), and I am, as the marginalia say, open to one project at a time.
manifesto.pullquote: A notebook accuracy of 92% is the beginning, never the verdict.

projects.title: The Counterfeit Face
projects.statement: Manipulated video is the cheapest lie on the internet. This study builds a deep-learning detector for image and video manipulation — a convolutional pipeline with deliberate pre-processing stages, trained to spot the counterfeit face rather than merely the visible artefact.
outcomes: End-to-end CNN pipeline with structured pre-processing
Evaluated on manipulated image & video sets
Architecture open on GitHub for reproduction

figure.caption: Architecture study — the counterfeit face is caught in the pipeline, not the frame.

projects.title: Sign Speak
projects.statement: A real-time hand-sign recognition system that turns annotated gestures into spoken meaning — built with OpenCV and MediaPipe for tracking and a TensorFlow CNN for classification. Selected from the cohort for the Edunet regional round, the project exists to make communication accessible where it is often assumed.
outcomes: Live gesture-to-text classification from camera input
92% trained accuracy on a custom annotated dataset
Selected for regional round at Edunet Foundation showcase

figure.caption: Fig. 02 — a frame from the field diary: thirty annotated hand classes, one stubborn framerate.

projects.title: Designing a Conversationalist
projects.statement: Reasoning models are as good as the context you give them. This assistant wraps the DeepSeek-R1 model from Hugging Face in a web interface with conversation history — exploring what it takes to turn a heavy open-weight model into something that remembers, continues, and holds a thread.
outcomes: Open-weight LLM behind a working web interface

figure.caption: Fig. 03 — thread study: how much memory does a conversation deserve?

projects.title: The Quiet Warning
projects.statement: Some predictions matter more than others. Stroke risk is one of them: a classification study over clinical features, comparing classical machine-learning models on a medical dataset — a reminder that the highest-impact models are often the most legible ones.
outcomes: Feature-driven risk scoring on medical data
Used as a teaching exercise for my ML assist class

figure.caption: Fig. 04 — an ROC study in warm ink; the quiet warning, drawn out.

about.title: Signed, sealed, still learning.
about.heading: An engineer who treats model-building as a discipline of annotation, patience and honest evaluation.
paragraphs: I am an applied AI developer with a product instinct and an engineer's patience. My work lives in computer vision and language systems — real-time gesture recognition, deepfake detection, predictive health models — built to survive real environments rather than demos.

I interned with Google's AI-ML virtual programme and researched at the Edunet Foundation, where Sign Speak — my hand-sign system — was selected for the regional round. Between internships I served as an ML teaching assistant at KIET, guided two dozen students through regression to neural networks, and discovered that teaching is the fastest way to find the holes in what you know.

I hold B.Tech in Computer Science (AI & ML), write in English, Telugu and Hindi, and keep eighteen Google Cloud badges as a quiet shelf of evidence. I am, at heart, someone who believes the model is finished only when it works in the world.

entries.title: On the shelf this month
entries.body: Sequences of transformers on three-line postcards — attention papers, the DeepSeek spec, a monograph on object detection history. Reading papers is annotating them; the margin is where the real work happens.

entries.title: YOLO vs. Faster R-CNN: an annotation diary
entries.body: A head-to-head on the same video set — not about the mAP, but about how much manual annotation each head actually demands. Conclusion so far: the framerate always wins the argument.

entries.title: Minimum viable intelligence
entries.body: A short essay on the gap between a model that classifies and a system that helps. The prosthetic is not the brain; it is the pipeline around it. Occasionally I rewrite a paragraph.

entries.title: The 92% problem
entries.body: A standing note on the difference between notebook accuracy and classroom reality — bad light, fast hands, marginal framerates. Every project gets a footnote against this page.
